t: 3672 — Sum of Weighted Modes in Subarrays
o: Slide a window of size k across nums; for each window compute mode × (mode's frequency) with the smallest value winning ties, and sum these weights. Naively each window costs O(k). Incrementally, adding/removing one element changes exactly one frequency by 1, so the maximum frequency can be maintained in O(1); a lazy min-heap per frequency level supplies the smallest value attaining that maximum.
k: Sliding the window changes one element's frequency by ±1, so the window max frequency is maintainable in O(1) via a frequency-of-frequency counter.
Store values in a lazy min-heap indexed by frequency; stale entries (whose current count differs) are popped on demand.
Total complexity O(n log n) versus O(nk) brute force.

a.n: Approach 1: Sliding window with frequency buckets and lazy heaps
a.i: Keep cnt[x] for the window, fc[f] = how many values currently have frequency f, and heaps[f] = min-heap of values that have ever reached frequency f inside the stream. On insert, push the value onto its new frequency heap and possibly raise maxF; on delete, if the departed frequency was the sole maximum, decrement maxF (frequencies shift by one, so this catches up correctly). At each window, clean heaps[maxF] of stale tops and add maxF × top.
s: Insert first k elements, updating cnt, fc, heaps, maxF.
Clean heaps[maxF]; add maxF × heap-top to the answer.
For each subsequent i: insert nums[i], remove nums[i−k], adjust maxF via fc, clean, accumulate.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def sumOfWeightedModes(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        import heapq
        from collections import defaultdict
        cnt = defaultdict(int); fc = defaultdict(int); heaps = defaultdict(list)
        maxF = 0; ans = 0
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            f = cnt[x] + 1; cnt[x] = f
            fc[f - 1] -= 1; fc[f] += 1
            heaps[f].append(x)
            heapq.heapify(heaps[f]) if False else None
            heapq.heappush(heaps[f], x)
            if f > maxF: maxF = f
            if i >= k:
                y = nums[i - k]
                f = cnt[y] - 1; cnt[y] = f
                fc[f + 1] -= 1; fc[f] += 1
                if f + 1 == maxF and fc[maxF] == 0: maxF -= 1
            if i >= k - 1:
                h = heaps[maxF]
                while cnt[h[0]] != maxF:
                    heapq.heappop(h)
                ans += maxF * h[0]
        return ans

a.t: O(n log n) — each element is pushed to heaps a constant number of times; heap ops are logarithmic

a.i: Recount frequencies from scratch for every window with a hash map, then pick the smallest value among maximum frequencies. O(nk) time — perfectly clear, adequate for small inputs, too slow at n = 1e5 with large k.
s: For each window start, build a Counter of the k elements.
Find max frequency; among values achieving it take the smallest.

w: The lazy-heap trick avoids ordered sets (which Python lacks in stdlib): entries are inserted once per frequency gain and discarded only when they surface as a stale top, giving amortized efficiency. Pitfalls: forgetting that maxF must decrease gradually on removals (handled by the fc==0 check), tie-breaking to the smallest value, and 64-bit accumulation (weights up to 1e5 × 1e5 × 1e5 windows).
